two_sum.title: Two Sum
two_sum.question: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return indices of the two numbers such that they add up to target. You may assume that each input would have exactly one solution.
hints: Think about what information you need to store as you traverse the array.
For each number, you need to find its complement (target - num). How can you check this quickly?
A hashmap lets you look up previously seen numbers in O(1) time.
two_sum.optimal_explanation: Single pass hashmap. Store each number's index. For each num, check if complement exists. O(n) time, O(n) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Check every pair of numbers. Simple but slow for large inputs.

approaches.name: Hashmap
approaches.desc: Store each number's index. For each number check if complement exists. Single pass.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (sorted)
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
approaches.desc: Sort array, use two pointers. But loses original indices.

best_time_to_buy_stock.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
best_time_to_buy_stock.question: Given an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i, return the maximum profit you can achieve. You can only buy once and sell once. If no profit is possible, return 0.
hints: You want to buy low and sell high. Track the minimum price seen so far.
At each day, calculate profit if you sold today (price - min_so_far).
Track the maximum profit seen across all days.
best_time_to_buy_stock.optimal_explanation: One pass. Track min price seen so far. At each price compute potential profit. O(n) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Check every pair of buy/sell days. Very slow for large inputs.

approaches.name: Min Price Tracking
approaches.desc: Track min price seen so far. At each day compute profit = price - min. Single pass.

contains_duplicate.title: Contains Duplicate
contains_duplicate.question: Given an integer array nums, return True if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return False if every element is distinct.
hints: A brute force approach compares every pair — O(n²). Can you do better?
What data structure gives you O(1) lookup?
A set stores unique elements. If adding an element fails, it's a duplicate.
contains_duplicate.optimal_explanation: Convert to set (removes duplicates). If lengths differ, duplicates exist. O(n) time, O(n) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Compare every pair of elements. Very slow.

approaches.name: Sorting
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
approaches.desc: Sort array, check adjacent elements for duplicates.

approaches.name: HashSet
approaches.desc: Add each element to set. If already exists, duplicate found. Fastest approach.

approaches.name: One-liner Set
approaches.desc: Compare len(nums) with len(set(nums)). Most Pythonic.

product_except_self.title: Product of Array Except Self
product_except_self.question: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. You must solve it without using the division operator and in O(n) time.
hints: Think about prefix products and suffix products separately.
answer[i] = product of all elements to the LEFT × product of all elements to the RIGHT.
You can compute left products in one pass, then multiply by right products in another pass.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: For each element, multiply all others. Division not used but slow.

approaches.name: Prefix & Suffix
approaches.desc: answer[i] = product of all left × product of all right. Two passes.

approaches.name: Optimized (O(1) space)
approaches.desc: Build prefix in output array. Then multiply suffix on the fly. No extra array needed.

valid_anagram.title: Valid Anagram
valid_anagram.question: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses all the original letters exactly once.
hints: Two anagrams have the same character frequencies.
Count character frequencies in both strings and compare.
A hashmap or Counter from Python's collections module works perfectly here.
valid_anagram.optimal_explanation: Count character frequencies in both strings. Compare. O(n) time, O(1) space (at most 26 chars).

approaches.name: Sorting
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
approaches.desc: Sort both strings and compare. Simple but slower.

approaches.name: Frequency Counter
approaches.desc: Count character frequencies using array of 26. Compare counts. Fastest.

approaches.name: Counter (Python)
approaches.desc: Use Python Counter — Counter(s) == Counter(t). Most Pythonic.

longest_substring_without_repeating.title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
longest_substring_without_repeating.question: Given a string s, find the length of the longest substring without repeating characters.
hints: Think about a sliding window approach with two pointers.
Expand the right pointer, and when you see a duplicate, shrink from the left.
A hashmap can store the last seen index of each character for efficient shrinking.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Check all substrings for uniqueness. Very slow.

approaches.name: Sliding Window (Set)
approaches.desc: Two pointers with set. Shrink window when duplicate found.

approaches.name: Sliding Window (HashMap)
approaches.desc: Store last seen index of each char. Jump left pointer directly. More efficient.

reverse_linked_list.title: Reverse a Linked List
reverse_linked_list.question: Given the head of a singly linked list as an array (for simplicity), return the list reversed. Input: list of values. Output: reversed list of values.
hints: Think about what you need to track: previous node, current node, next node.
At each step: save next, point current to previous, advance both pointers.
Iterative reversal uses O(1) extra space. Recursive uses O(n) stack space.

approaches.name: Iterative
approaches.desc: Three pointers: prev, curr, next. Reverse links one by one. Best approach.

approaches.name: Recursive
approaches.desc: Recursively reverse rest, then fix current link. Uses call stack.

maximum_subarray.title: Maximum Subarray (Kadane's Algorithm)
maximum_subarray.question: Given an integer array nums, find the contiguous subarray which has the largest sum and return its sum.
hints: A brute force checks all subarrays — O(n²). Kadane's algorithm does it in O(n).
At each position, decide: should I extend the previous subarray or start fresh?
current_sum = max(num, current_sum + num). Track the global maximum.
maximum_subarray.optimal_explanation: Kadane's algorithm. At each step: extend or start fresh. O(n) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Check all subarrays and track maximum sum.

approaches.name: Kadane's Algorithm
approaches.desc: At each step decide: extend current subarray or start fresh.

approaches.name: Divide & Conquer
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
approaches.desc: Split array, find max in left, right, and crossing middle.

climbing_stairs.title: Climbing Stairs
climbing_stairs.question: You are climbing a staircase. It takes n steps to reach the top. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. In how many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
hints: Think recursively: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
This is Fibonacci! dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
You only need the last two values — optimize space to O(1).
climbing_stairs.optimal_explanation: Fibonacci with O(1) space. Only keep last two values. O(n) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Recursion (naive)
approaches.desc: Pure recursion — exponential time due to repeated subproblems.

approaches.name: Memoization (top-down)
approaches.desc: Cache results of subproblems to avoid recomputation.

approaches.name: DP (bottom-up)
approaches.desc: Only keep last 2 values. Fibonacci pattern.

coin_change.title: Coin Change
coin_change.question: Given an array of coin denominations and an amount, return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount. Return -1 if it cannot be done.
hints: This is a classic bottom-up DP problem.
dp[i] = minimum coins to make amount i.
For each amount, try every coin: dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - coin] + 1).
coin_change.optimal_explanation: Bottom-up DP. dp[i] = min coins for amount i. Try every coin at each amount. O(amount×coins) time.

approaches.name: Brute Force (recursion)
approaches.desc: Try all combinations. Extremely slow for large amounts.

approaches.name: Top-down DP (memoization)
approaches.desc: Recursion + cache. Store results of subproblems.

approaches.name: Bottom-up DP
approaches.desc: Build solution from amount 0 to target. Most efficient.

binary_search.title: Binary Search
binary_search.question: Given a sorted array of integers nums and an integer target, write a function to search for target. Return its index if found, or -1 if not found. Must be O(log n).
hints: Split the search space in half each time.
If nums[mid] == target, return mid. If less, search right. If more, search left.
Be careful with integer overflow: mid = left + (right - left) // 2.
binary_search.optimal_solution:
def solve(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums)-1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi-lo)//2
        if nums[mid] == target: return mid
        elif nums[mid] < target: lo = mid+1
        else: hi = mid-1
    return -1
binary_search.optimal_explanation: Classic binary search. lo+(hi-lo)//2 avoids overflow. O(log n) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Linear Search
approaches.desc: Check each element one by one. Works but slow.

approaches.name: Binary Search (iterative)
approaches.desc: Divide search space in half each iteration. Best approach.

approaches.name: Binary Search (recursive)
approaches.complexity: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
approaches.desc: Same logic but uses call stack for recursion.

valid_parentheses.title: Valid Parentheses
valid_parentheses.question: Given a string s containing just '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. Brackets must be closed in the correct order.
hints: A stack is perfect for matching opening and closing brackets.
Push opening brackets. When you see a closing bracket, check if it matches the top of the stack.
At the end, the stack must be empty for the string to be valid.
valid_parentheses.optimal_explanation: Stack-based matching. Push opening brackets. On closing bracket, check top matches. O(n) time, O(n) space.

approaches.name: Counter approach
approaches.desc: Count opens and closes. But fails for mixed brackets like '([)]'.

approaches.name: Stack approach
approaches.desc: Push opening brackets, pop and match on closing. Handles all cases.

min_stack.title: Min Stack
min_stack.question: Implement a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element in O(1) time. Input is a list of operations like ['push:5','push:3','min','pop','min']. Return list of results for 'top' and 'min' operations.
hints: Use two stacks: one for values, one to track minimums.
When pushing, also push to min_stack if value <= current minimum.
When popping, if popped value equals min_stack top, pop min_stack too.

approaches.name: Two Stacks
approaches.desc: One stack for values, one for minimums. Push to min_stack only when value <= current min.

approaches.name: Single Stack with pairs
approaches.desc: Store (value, current_min) pairs in one stack. Simpler implementation.

number_of_islands.title: Number of Islands
number_of_islands.question: Given an m x n 2D binary grid representing a map of 1s (land) and 0s (water), return the number of islands. An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically.
hints: Think about graph traversal. Each island is a connected component of 1s.
When you find a 1, do a DFS/BFS to mark all connected land as visited.
Count how many times you start a fresh DFS — that's your answer.
number_of_islands.optimal_explanation: DFS from each unvisited land cell. Mark visited by changing '1' to '0'. Count DFS starts. O(m×n) time.

approaches.name: DFS
approaches.desc: For each unvisited land cell, do DFS to mark entire island. Count DFS calls.

approaches.name: BFS
approaches.desc: Same idea but uses queue instead of recursion. Avoids recursion limit issues.

approaches.name: Union Find
approaches.desc: Advanced — union adjacent land cells. Count components. Best for dynamic graphs.

invert_binary_tree.title: Invert Binary Tree
invert_binary_tree.question: Given a binary tree as a level-order list (None for missing nodes), invert the tree and return the level-order list.
hints: At each node, swap the left and right children.
Recursively invert both subtrees.
This can also be done iteratively using a queue (BFS).

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.desc: At each node swap left and right, then recurse. Simplest approach.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS
approaches.desc: Use queue, process level by level, swap children at each node.

max_depth_binary_tree.title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
max_depth_binary_tree.question: Given a binary tree as a level-order list, return its maximum depth (number of nodes along the longest path from root to leaf).
hints: Think recursively: max_depth(node) = 1 + max(max_depth(left), max_depth(right)).
Base case: if node is None, depth is 0.
Can also be solved with BFS, counting levels.

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.desc: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). Simplest.

approaches.name: Iterative BFS
approaches.desc: Level-order traversal. Count levels. Each level = +1 depth.

approaches.name: Iterative DFS (Stack)
approaches.desc: Use stack to simulate recursion. Track max depth seen.

merge_two_sorted_lists.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
merge_two_sorted_lists.question: Given two sorted arrays (representing linked lists), merge them into one sorted array.
hints: Use two pointers, one for each list.
Compare the current elements of both lists and take the smaller one.
Don't forget to append remaining elements from the non-empty list.

approaches.name: Two Pointers (Iterative)
approaches.desc: Compare heads, take smaller, advance that pointer. Best approach.

approaches.name: Recursive
approaches.desc: Pick smaller head, recurse on rest. Clean but uses call stack.

three_sum.title: 3Sum
three_sum.question: Given an integer array nums, return all the triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] such that i != j != k, and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. The solution must not contain duplicate triplets.
hints: Sort the array first — this lets you use two pointers efficiently.
Fix one element, then use two pointers on the remaining sorted subarray.
Skip duplicates carefully to avoid duplicate triplets in the result.
three_sum.optimal_solution:
def solve(nums):
    nums.sort()
    res = []
    for i in range(len(nums)-2):
        if i>0 and nums[i]==nums[i-1]: continue
        l,r = i+1,len(nums)-1
        while l<r:
            s = nums[i]+nums[l]+nums[r]
            if s==0: res.append([nums[i],nums[l],nums[r]]); l+=1; r-=1
            elif s<0: l+=1
            else: r-=1
    return res
three_sum.optimal_explanation: Sort + two pointers. Fix one element, use two pointers for rest. Skip duplicates. O(n²) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Check all triplets. Way too slow for large inputs.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers
approaches.desc: Sort array. Fix one element, use two pointers for rest. Skip duplicates carefully.

approaches.name: HashSet
approaches.desc: Fix one element, use hashset for complement. Harder to handle duplicates.

find_median_sorted_arrays.title: Find Median of Two Sorted Arrays
find_median_sorted_arrays.question: Given two sorted arrays nums1 and nums2, return the median of the two sorted arrays combined. The overall run time complexity should be O(log(m+n)).
hints: Merging both arrays naively is O(m+n). Think binary search.
Binary search on the smaller array to find the correct partition point.
After partitioning, max_left elements must be <= min_right elements on both sides.

approaches.name: Merge & Find
approaches.desc: Merge both arrays, find middle element. Simple but not optimal.

approaches.name: Binary Search
approaches.desc: Binary search on smaller array to find correct partition. Optimal solution.

word_search.title: Word Search
word_search.question: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word exists in the grid. The word can be constructed from sequentially adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically). Each cell may not be used more than once.
hints: Use DFS/backtracking starting from every cell that matches word[0].
Mark cells as visited during DFS, then unmark when backtracking.
Check all 4 directions (up, down, left, right) at each step.

approaches.name: DFS + Backtracking
approaches.desc: Start DFS from each matching cell. Mark visited, explore 4 directions, unmark on backtrack.

approaches.name: Trie + DFS
approaches.desc: Advanced — used when searching multiple words. Build trie, then DFS.

house_robber.title: House Robber
house_robber.question: You are a robber planning to rob houses along a street. Adjacent houses have security systems that alert police if both are robbed. Given an array nums representing money in each house, return the maximum amount you can rob without robbing adjacent houses.
hints: At each house, you have two choices: rob it (add to prev_prev) or skip it (take prev).
dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).
You only need the previous two values — optimize space to O(1).
house_robber.optimal_explanation: DP with O(1) space. prev1=best including current, prev2=best excluding. O(n) time, O(1) space.

approaches.name: Brute Force
approaches.desc: Try all possible combinations of houses.

approaches.name: DP with array
approaches.desc: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).

approaches.name: DP optimized
approaches.desc: Only keep two variables — prev2 and prev1.

top_k_frequent_elements.title: Top K Frequent Elements
top_k_frequent_elements.question: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.
hints: Count frequencies using a hashmap.
Then find the top-k elements by frequency.
Bucket sort by frequency gives O(n) time — frequencies range from 1 to n.

approaches.name: Sort by frequency
approaches.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
approaches.desc: Count frequencies, sort by count, take top k.

approaches.name: Min Heap
approaches.complexity: O(n log k) time, O(n) space
approaches.desc: Count frequencies, maintain heap of size k. Better when k << n.

approaches.name: Bucket Sort
approaches.desc: Frequencies range 1 to n. Use index as frequency bucket. Linear time.
